question: do i have to pay back everything on my financial aid offer? some of it says grant and some says loan
answer: Not everything. Grants and scholarships are generally money you don't repay; StudentAid.gov notes that a Federal Pell Grant doesn't need to be repaid except in rare circumstances. Loans must be paid back, with interest, even though they appear in the same list. Work-study isn't paid up front at all: it's a chance to earn money through a job, and the income isn't guaranteed. When you read your offer, sort every line into these three groups before you add anything up.

sources.title: How To Evaluate Your Aid Offers (StudentAid.gov)
Financial Aid Dictionary (StudentAid.gov)

question: My aid offer says total aid is more than tuition. Does that mean I'm basically going for free?
answer: Not necessarily. A "total aid" figure usually adds together grants, loans you'll have to repay and work-study you'd have to earn, so it can look much bigger than what you actually get to keep. Tuition is also only one part of the cost; the cost of attendance includes food and housing, books, transportation and other expenses. A better number is your net price: the cost of attendance minus only your grants and scholarships. Ask your financial aid office to walk you through any line you aren't sure about.

sources.title: How To Evaluate Your Aid Offers (StudentAid.gov)
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 2, Ch. 6: Consumer Information and School Reporting
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 3, Ch. 2: Cost of Attendance (Budget)

question: What's the difference between a college's sticker price and its net price?
answer: The sticker price is the published cost before any aid. Net price is the cost of attendance minus the grant and scholarship aid you receive, so it's an estimate of what you'd pay out of pocket, whether from savings, earnings or loans. Two schools with very different sticker prices can end up with similar net prices. StudentAid.gov's advice is to always compare net price, not sticker price.

sources.title: How To Evaluate Your Aid Offers (StudentAid.gov)
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 2, Ch. 6: Consumer Information and School Reporting
Financial Aid Dictionary (StudentAid.gov)

question: why is my cost of attendance so much higher than what the school actually bills me?
answer: Your cost of attendance (COA) is an estimate of the full cost of a year at that school, not just your bill. Besides tuition and fees, it can include food and housing, books, course materials, supplies and equipment, transportation, and miscellaneous personal expenses, plus items like dependent care or disability-related costs when they apply. The school sets reasonable amounts for each category and can use averages, so some of these are allowances for expenses you pay somewhere else, not charges on your account. Your aid can't exceed this COA, which is why it matters even for costs the school doesn't bill.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 3, Ch. 2: Cost of Attendance (Budget)
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 3, Ch. 3: Packaging Aid
sources.section: Packaging: total aid cannot exceed COA

question: Award letter splits costs into 'direct' and 'indirect'. What does that mean for what I actually owe?
answer: Schools label these differently, but the useful split is between charges the school puts on your account, such as tuition, fees and school-provided food and housing, and the rest of your cost of attendance, such as books, transportation and personal expenses, which you pay on your own. Your aid is applied to the billed charges first. What you owe the school is the billed charges minus the aid that's actually credited, while the other costs are estimates you'll need to budget for. If the offer doesn't make the split clear, ask the financial aid or billing office which items will appear on your bill.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 4, Ch. 2: Disbursing Title IV Funds
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 3, Ch. 2: Cost of Attendance (Budget)

question: Does my cost of attendance include money for a laptop?
answer: It can. Federal rules let a school include a reasonable allowance for renting or buying a personal computer in the books, course materials, supplies and equipment part of your cost of attendance. Each school decides how much to allow. If your program requires equipment that costs more than the standard allowance, you can ask the financial aid office whether it will review your COA case by case, but expect to show documentation.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 3, Ch. 2: Cost of Attendance (Budget)
sources.section: Books, course materials, supplies, and equipment; Professional judgment adjustments

question: I have a kid and pay for daycare so I can go to class. Can my school add that to my cost of attendance?
answer: Dependent care is one of the categories the law allows in a cost of attendance, so it's worth asking. Contact your school's financial aid office, explain your childcare costs, and ask how to request a cost of attendance adjustment; they will likely ask for receipts or other documentation. Adjustments are made case by case and the aid administrator decides whether to approve one. A higher COA can raise the amount of aid you're eligible for, though it doesn't guarantee more grant money.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 3, Ch. 2: Cost of Attendance (Budget)
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases

question: Do I have to accept every part of my financial aid offer?
answer: No. You can accept the aid you want and turn down the rest, and loans in particular are optional: you can take a smaller amount or none at all. StudentAid.gov's advice is to use grants and scholarships first, then work-study, then loans, and to follow the school's directions to accept your offer on time. Even after a loan is paid to your account, you have the right to cancel all or part of it within the window in the notice your school sends you.

sources.title: How To Evaluate Your Aid Offers (StudentAid.gov)
sources.section: Accepting aid and order to consider aid

sources.title: 34 CFR 668.165: Notices and authorizations
sources.section: Right to cancel all or a portion of a loan

question: I accepted my student loan but now I don't want it and it's already on my account. Can I still cancel?
answer: Often yes. When your school credits a loan to your account, it has to send you a notice explaining your right to cancel all or part of it and the deadline. If your request arrives in time, the school must return the money and cancel the loan: that's by the later of the first day of the payment period or 14 days after the notice if the school got your confirmation in advance, or within 30 days of the notice otherwise. The school may still be able to honor a later request, so contact the financial aid office as soon as you decide.

sources.title: 34 CFR 668.165: Notices and authorizations
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 4, Ch. 2: Disbursing Title IV Funds

question: when does my financial aid actually get paid out, all at once or in pieces?
answer: In pieces. Federal aid other than work-study is paid by payment period, and at a school with semesters or quarters each term is a payment period, so your yearly aid is usually split across terms. The money goes to your school account first and pays your tuition, fees and school housing and food charges. Work-study is different: it's paid as wages for hours you work. Your school's financial aid office or bursar can tell you its disbursement dates.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 3, Ch. 1: Academic Years, Academic Calendars, Payment Periods, and Disbursements
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 4, Ch. 2: Disbursing Title IV Funds

question: How early before classes can my school release my financial aid?
answer: For credit-hour programs with substantially equal terms, the earliest a school can disburse federal aid is 10 days before the first day of classes in the payment period. Other kinds of programs, like clock-hour or non-term programs, have different rules tied to completing the previous payment period. Within those limits each school sets its own dates, so check with your financial aid office for yours.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 4, Ch. 2: Disbursing Title IV Funds

question: freshman here, why is my loan still pending a few weeks into the semester when my grant already paid?
answer: This is normal for many first-year students. If you're a first-year, first-time Direct Loan borrower, a school generally can't disburse your loan until 30 days after your program begins. Some schools with low cohort default rates are exempt from this delay, so not every school does it. Your grant isn't covered by that rule, which is why it may have arrived first; ask the financial aid office for your expected loan date.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 4, Ch. 2: Disbursing Title IV Funds

question: when do i get my financial aid refund? the bursar just says 'soon'
answer: A federal aid credit balance happens when your federal aid for a payment period is more than your allowable charges. The school must pay it to you as soon as possible and no later than 14 days after the first day of classes, if the balance existed by then, or 14 days after the balance occurs, if that's later. Balances under one dollar don't have to be paid. If you've signed an authorization letting the school hold your credit balance, different rules apply, so check whether you signed one.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 4, Ch. 2: Disbursing Title IV Funds

question: My school wants me to sign a form letting them hold my leftover aid. Do I have to sign it?
answer: No. A school can hold a credit balance only with your written authorization, and it can't require or pressure you to give it. If you do sign, you can cancel or change the authorization at any time; after a cancellation, the school must pay you the held funds within 14 days. Even with an authorization, the school must pay any remaining loan funds by the end of the loan period and other federal aid by the end of the last payment period in the award year.

sources.title: 34 CFR 668.165: Notices and authorizations
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 4, Ch. 2: Disbursing Title IV Funds

question: Can my school take my aid to pay a parking ticket or my balance from last year?
answer: Only in limited ways without your permission. A school can use federal aid for tuition, fees and school-provided food and housing, but it needs your authorization to pay other educationally related charges, such as parking or fines. For charges from a prior award year, it can use current-year aid without authorization only up to a total of $200 for tuition, fees and food and housing; anything more requires your authorization. Ask your bursar what authorizations you've signed.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 4, Ch. 2: Disbursing Title IV Funds

question: my aid won't pay out until classes start but I need my textbooks before then. what can I do?
answer: Ask your financial aid office about the books and supplies rule. If your aid could have been paid 10 days before the term and would have left you a credit balance, the school must give you a way to get your required books and supplies by the seventh day of the payment period, for example a bookstore credit or an early payment. You can decline it, and it doesn't apply if a first-year, first-time Direct Loan is your only aid and the 30-day delay applies.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 4, Ch. 2: Disbursing Title IV Funds

question: what is SAP and how can it make me lose financial aid?
answer: Satisfactory Academic Progress (SAP) is the set of standards your school uses to decide whether you're making enough progress to keep getting federal aid. It has three parts: a grade standard (GPA), a pace standard comparing the credits you complete with the credits you attempt, and a maximum timeframe for finishing your program. If you don't meet the standards when your school checks, you can lose eligibility for federal aid until you meet them again or win an appeal. Every school publishes its own SAP policy, so look it up on the financial aid office's website.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements
Financial Aid Dictionary (StudentAid.gov)

question: Is there a limit on how long I can get federal aid while working on my bachelor's?
answer: Yes. For undergraduate programs measured in credit hours, the maximum timeframe can be no longer than 150% of the published length of the program. For a 120-credit degree, that means up to 180 attempted credits. You stop meeting this standard as soon as it becomes mathematically impossible to finish within the limit, not only when you reach it. Your school's SAP policy explains how it counts transfer credits, repeats and withdrawals.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements
34 CFR 668.34: Satisfactory academic progress

question: my gpa is fine but the school says I'm failing SAP because of 'pace'. what does that mean?
answer: Pace is the share of the credits you attempt that you actually complete. Your school's policy sets the minimum, and it's there to make sure you'll finish within the maximum timeframe. Withdrawals after the add/drop period count as attempted but not completed, so a few W's or failed classes can pull your pace down even with a good GPA. Check the exact calculation in your school's SAP policy and ask the aid office what you'd need to complete to get back on track.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: What GPA do I need to keep my federal financial aid?
answer: Your school sets the exact requirement in its SAP policy. Federal rules set a floor: for programs longer than two academic years, by the end of your second academic year you must have at least a C average or its equivalent, or academic standing consistent with your school's graduation requirements. Many schools check GPA more often and set their own minimums, so read your school's policy rather than relying on a general number.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements
34 CFR 668.34: Satisfactory academic progress

question: I got a 'financial aid warning' email. Do I need to appeal something right now?
answer: Usually not yet. Financial aid warning is a status some schools give automatically when they check SAP at the end of every payment period: you keep your aid for one more payment period without having to appeal. If you still don't meet the standards at the end of that period, you'll lose eligibility unless you appeal successfully. Use the warning period to talk with an advisor and the financial aid office about what you need to complete.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements
34 CFR 668.34: Satisfactory academic progress

question: How do I write a SAP appeal?
answer: First check that your school allows appeals, because that's the school's choice. An appeal can be based on things like your own injury or illness, the death of a relative, or other special circumstances, and it has to explain why you didn't make SAP and what has changed that will let you meet the standards. Attach documentation, such as medical or other records, and follow the school's form and deadline. If you're approved, you'll usually be on financial aid probation or an academic plan.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements
34 CFR 668.34: Satisfactory academic progress

question: What's an academic plan for SAP and what happens if I don't follow it?
answer: If your school approves your SAP appeal but you can't meet the standards in a single payment period, the school and you develop an academic plan. The plan lays out what you must do and by when, so you'll meet the SAP standards by a specific point or complete your program. If you don't meet the plan's terms when the school reviews it, you can lose your aid eligibility. Changing the plan requires a new appeal.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: If I pay for a semester out of pocket, will that get my financial aid back after failing SAP?
answer: No. Paying for classes yourself, or sitting out a term, doesn't change your SAP status by itself. Unless you're on warning, probation or an academic plan, you regain eligibility only by doing something that brings you back into compliance with the standards, like raising your GPA or completion rate. Paying for a term can help if it lets you complete classes that meet the standards, but the classes are what count, not the payment. You can also ask whether an appeal is possible.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: Do transfer credits count against me for the SAP time limit?
answer: They can. Transfer credits that apply to your current program count in the pace and maximum timeframe calculations. Your school's SAP policy has to explain how it treats transfer credits, repeated courses, incompletes and withdrawals. If you're changing majors or transferring, ask the aid office how many attempted credits you'll start with.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements
sources.section: Transfer credits, repeats, withdrawals and incompletes

question: What's Return of Title IV funds? I'm thinking about withdrawing in the middle of the semester.
answer: Return of Title IV funds (R2T4) is the federal rule for what happens to your federal aid when you withdraw before finishing a payment period. Your school calculates how much aid you earned based on how much of the period you completed, and the unearned part has to be returned. That can leave you owing your school money, because the school's own refund policy for tuition is separate. Before withdrawing, ask the financial aid office to estimate the result for your situation.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 5, Ch. 1: General Requirements for Withdrawals and the Return of Title IV Funds
34 CFR 668.22: Treatment of Title IV funds when a student withdraws

question: if i withdraw after 60% of the semester do i keep all my aid?
answer: For federal aid, yes. Once you've completed more than 60% of the payment period, you're considered to have earned 100% of the federal aid you received and were scheduled to receive, so none of it is unearned. Before that point you earn aid in proportion to the share of the period you completed. Separately, your school's own tuition refund policy may still matter, and withdrawing can affect your SAP, so talk to the aid office first.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 5, Ch. 1: General Requirements for Withdrawals and the Return of Title IV Funds
34 CFR 668.22: Treatment of Title IV funds when a student withdraws

question: How does my school figure out what share of my aid I 'earned' if I leave mid-term?
answer: For credit-hour programs, the school divides the number of calendar days you completed in the payment period by the total calendar days in it, and the day you withdrew counts as completed. Scheduled breaks of five or more consecutive days are left out of both numbers. That percentage is the share of aid you earned, up to the 60% point, after which you've earned it all. The school's financial aid office runs this calculation and can show it to you.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 5, Ch. 2: The Steps in the Return of Title IV Aid Calculation, Part 1
sources.section: Step 2: Percentage of payment period completed

sources.title: 34 CFR 668.22: Treatment of Title IV funds when a student withdraws

question: If I drop one class, does the Return of Title IV thing kick in?
answer: Not usually. Dropping some classes while you stay enrolled in others is a change in your enrollment status, not a withdrawal, so R2T4 doesn't apply. It does apply if you drop or stop attending all of your aid-eligible classes. A drop can still change your aid in other ways: your Pell Grant may be recalculated, and you need at least half-time enrollment for Direct Loans. Ask the aid office before you drop.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 5, Ch. 1: General Requirements for Withdrawals and the Return of Title IV Funds

question: I stopped going to my classes but never officially withdrew. What happens with my aid?
answer: Stopping attendance without telling the school is treated as an unofficial withdrawal, and R2T4 still applies. If you didn't notify the school, it can use the midpoint of the payment period as your withdrawal date, or, at a school not required to take attendance, your last documented academically related activity. Unearned aid then has to be returned, which can leave you owing the school. If you're still in the term, talk to your school before you stop attending.

sources.title: 34 CFR 668.22: Treatment of Title IV funds when a student withdraws
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 5, Ch. 1: General Requirements for Withdrawals and the Return of Title IV Funds

question: After my school sends back my unearned aid, do I personally owe anything for my Pell Grant?
answer: Possibly a small amount. After the school returns its share, you might owe part of the remaining grant overpayment, but only the part that exceeds 50% of the total grant aid disbursed (or that could have been) for the period, and you don't repay an overpayment of $50 or less per grant program. If you owe, you keep your aid eligibility for 45 days after the school's notice, and you can repay in full or sign a repayment agreement. Unearned loan money you received is repaid normally under your loan's terms.

question: Can I end up owing my college money after I withdraw even though aid covered my whole bill?
answer: Yes. The R2T4 rules decide how much federal aid you earned, while your school's own refund policy decides how much tuition and other charges you still owe, and the two are separate. If the school has to return unearned aid that had paid your charges, that part of your bill can come back to you as a debt. Your school must publish its withdrawal and refund policies, so read them and ask the bursar before you withdraw.

question: I heard there's a new rule where if you withdraw early the school can treat it like you never attended. Is that real?
answer: Yes, there's a new optional exemption. Under final regulations published January 3, 2025, effective July 1, 2026 (schools could start using it as of February 3, 2025), a student who withdraws isn't treated as withdrawn for R2T4 if the school treats them as never having attended, returns all the federal grant and loan aid, refunds all institutional charges, and cancels any balance created by that return. It's the school's choice, case by case, and if any condition isn't met the normal R2T4 process applies. Ask your aid office whether it uses this exemption.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 5, Ch. 1: General Requirements for Withdrawals and the Return of Title IV Funds
34 CFR 668.22: Treatment of Title IV funds when a student withdraws

question: Does the Return of Title IV calculation take back work-study money I already earned?
answer: No. The R2T4 rules don't apply to Federal Work-Study. Work-study is paid as wages for work you've done, so it isn't part of the earned-versus-unearned calculation. Your grants and loans for the period are what the calculation covers.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 5, Ch. 1: General Requirements for Withdrawals and the Return of Title IV Funds
sources.section: General Title IV principles: Federal Work-Study

question: after I withdraw, can I still get aid that hadn't paid out yet?
answer: Possibly. If the R2T4 calculation shows you earned more aid than was disbursed, you may be owed a post-withdrawal disbursement. For loan money, the school must notify you within 30 days of determining that you withdrew and give you at least 14 days to respond, because you can decline it. Grant money owed to you directly must be paid within 45 days. Watch for that notice and answer it on time.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 5, Ch. 1: General Requirements for Withdrawals and the Return of Title IV Funds

question: My parents' income dropped a lot since the year on our FAFSA. Can my school change my aid?
answer: You can ask. Financial aid administrators can use professional judgment to adjust the information in your aid calculation or your cost of attendance for special circumstances, such as a change in employment or income, or medical expenses not covered by insurance. Contact your school's financial aid office, explain what changed, and be ready to send documentation. The decision is up to the school, and it's final.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases
7 Options if You Didn't Receive Enough Financial Aid (StudentAid.gov)

question: My school denied my special circumstances request. Can I appeal to the Department of Education?
answer: No. A financial aid administrator's decision on a professional judgment adjustment is final and can't be appealed to the Department of Education. What you can do is ask the school why it was denied and whether more documentation would change the outcome. Schools can deny an individual request, but they can't have a policy of denying all special circumstance requests.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases
7 Options if You Didn't Receive Enough Financial Aid (StudentAid.gov)

question: What can a professional judgment appeal actually change, and what can't it change?
answer: Professional judgment lets an aid administrator adjust parts of your cost of attendance, or the data used to figure your Student Aid Index and Pell eligibility, when your circumstances justify it. A dependency override, from dependent to independent, is a separate case-by-case decision. Professional judgment can't be used to waive basic eligibility requirements or to change the federal formula itself. Each adjustment has to be documented, and the school decides.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases

question: I got a scholarship from a local club after my aid offer came out. Do I need to tell my financial aid office?
answer: Yes. Outside scholarships count as other financial assistance, and your school has to take them into account in your package. If the new money pushes your aid over your financial need, the school adjusts your package, and the handbook tells schools to reduce borrowing first, starting with unsubsidized loans. Report it to the aid office and ask how it will change your offer.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 3, Ch. 3: Packaging Aid
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 4, Ch. 3: Overawards and Overpayments

question: Will an outside scholarship lower my Pell Grant?
answer: Usually not. A correctly calculated Pell Grant isn't reduced because of other aid, and schools adjust other parts of your package, often loans, instead. The exception starting with 2026-27: if your non-federal grant and scholarship aid equals or exceeds your cost of attendance, the school must either reduce that non-federal aid below your COA or return your Pell Grant and cancel future disbursements. Students who qualify for a maximum Pell under the special rule for children of fallen servicemembers or public safety officers are exempt.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 3, Ch. 3: Packaging Aid

question: What's an overaward, and will I have to pay money back?
answer: An overaward happens when your aid adds up to more than your financial need or your cost of attendance, often because of a scholarship that came in after packaging. The school tries to fix it by adjusting aid that hasn't been paid yet; for campus-based aid it doesn't have to make a change if the overaward is $300 or less and the school didn't know about the extra funds. If the overaward isn't fixed before money is paid, it becomes an overpayment, and you can be responsible for one of $25 or more unless the school caused it. Report outside aid early to avoid this.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 4, Ch. 3: Overawards and Overpayments
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 3, Ch. 3: Packaging Aid

question: is work study paid as a lump sum like my grants?
answer: No. Federal Work-Study is paid as wages for hours you actually work, usually through a paycheck, and schools must pay you at least once a month. You earn at least the federal minimum wage. The amount on your aid offer is the most you can earn, not money that lands on your account. If you want your earnings applied to your school bill, you have to give the school separate written authorization.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 6, Ch. 2: The Federal Work-Study Program
sources.section: Payment of FWS compensation; minimum wage; crediting a student's account

question: Can I use my work-study award to pay my tuition bill at the start of the semester?
answer: Not up front. Work-study isn't credited to your account when the term starts; you earn it as you work. That means you'll need another way to cover your bill at the start of the term, such as grants, loans or a payment plan. You can authorize the school to credit your work-study wages to your account as you earn them, which can help with later balances.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 6, Ch. 2: The Federal Work-Study Program
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 3, Ch. 1: Academic Years, Academic Calendars, Payment Periods, and Disbursements

question: Work-study is on my aid offer but I can't find a job. Do I just lose it?
answer: Work-study is an opportunity to earn money, not a guaranteed amount; StudentAid.gov notes that work-study income isn't guaranteed. Schools must make jobs reasonably available to eligible students as far as funds allow, so contact your financial aid office or student employment office about open positions. There are no federal limits on hours per week, but you can't work during your scheduled class times, and your total earnings can't go past your award. If you don't earn it, ask the aid office whether other aid could fill the gap.

question: If I go part-time in spring 2027, will my federal student loan limit go down?
answer: Likely yes. Under Public Law 119-21 and a final rule published May 1, 2026, for periods of enrollment that begin on or after July 1, 2026, schools must reduce your annual Direct Loan limit in direct proportion to how far below full-time you are, rounded to the nearest whole percent. In an Education Department example, a student enrolled for half the full-time credits had the limit cut by 50%. It applies to term-based programs but not clock-hour or non-term programs, and Parent PLUS isn't affected. Your school's full-time definition is the baseline, so ask the aid office what your limit would be.

sources.title: FAQs: Reducing Annual Loan Limits for Less-Than-Full-Time Enrollment (FSA Partner Connect, August 2026)
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: If I drop a class after my Pell Grant pays out, will it get recalculated?
answer: It depends on timing and your school's policy. If you hadn't yet started attending all your classes, the school must recalculate your Pell for that payment period based on your lower enrollment. If you'd already attended all of them, recalculation isn't required by federal rules, but your school may have a written policy to do it, often with a cutoff date such as the end of add/drop. Ask the aid office about its Pell recalculation date before you drop.

question: what happens to my federal loans if I drop below half time?
answer: You have to be enrolled at least half-time to receive Direct Subsidized, Unsubsidized and PLUS loans, so dropping below half-time can stop future loan disbursements for that period. Your school defines full-time and half-time within federal minimums; for undergraduates at semester or quarter schools, full-time can't be less than 12 credit hours per term. Check your school's definitions and talk to the financial aid office before dropping, because it can also affect other aid.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: I'm transferring to a different college for spring. Does my financial aid move with me?
answer: Not automatically. Add your new school to your FAFSA through StudentAid.gov so it receives your information, and contact its financial aid office about its own forms and deadlines. Before paying you federal aid, the new school has to check your financial aid history, including any Pell you've already used this year and loan limits you may have reached. Ask the new school what aid it can offer for the rest of the year.

question: Can I get a full year of Pell at my new school if I already got Pell at my old school this year?
answer: Not a full new year's worth. Your new school figures your remaining Pell eligibility for the award year by subtracting the share of your Scheduled Award you already used, from 100% (or 150% if you qualify for year-round Pell). You can then receive Pell up to that remaining amount. If you end up receiving more than your Scheduled Award across schools in the same year, you may have to repay the excess.

question: What is a net price calculator and should I trust the number it gives me?
answer: A net price calculator is a tool most colleges must post on their websites that estimates your net price: the cost of attendance minus the grants and scholarships a student like you might receive. It's only an estimate. By law it has to say the result isn't a final award and isn't binding, and that you must complete the FAFSA to get an actual federal aid award. Use it to compare schools early, then compare the real aid offers when they arrive.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 2, Ch. 6: Consumer Information and School Reporting

question: How should I compare aid offers from different colleges?
answer: Start with each school's full cost of attendance, then subtract only the grants and scholarships to get the net price, and compare those numbers rather than sticker prices. Then look at what's left: how much would come from work-study you'd have to earn and loans you'd have to repay. The Department of Education recommends that offers show the full cost, list grants, loans and work-study separately, and show the estimated net cost. If two offers are hard to compare, ask each school's financial aid office to explain them.

sources.title: How To Evaluate Your Aid Offers (StudentAid.gov)
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 2, Ch. 6: Consumer Information and School Reporting

question: If I appeal my SAP because I was sick last semester, will they approve it?
answer: I can't predict that, because your school decides each appeal under its own SAP policy. What makes an appeal strong is the federal requirement itself: you explain why you didn't make SAP, such as an illness, and what has changed that will let you meet the standards, with documentation. The school may approve, approve with an academic plan, or deny. Your financial aid office can tell you what it looks for and the deadline.

question: Can you help me word my special circumstances letter so it says my mom lost her job? She didn't, but it'd get me more aid.
answer: I can't help with that, because a professional judgment request has to be based on real circumstances, and the school asks for documentation to support it. Giving false information to get federal aid isn't allowed. If your family's finances really have changed in other ways, like lower income or big medical bills, I can help you explain those honestly. You can also ask the aid office about other options, like payment plans or scholarships.

question: How much more aid will I get if I ask my school to raise my cost of attendance for car repairs?
answer: I can't tell you an amount, because the school decides whether to make any adjustment and what you'd be eligible for afterward. Transportation is an allowable COA category, but the cost of buying a vehicle isn't, and the aid administrator decides case by case, with documentation, whether a cost fits. Even when a COA goes up, the extra eligibility is often in loans rather than grants. Ask your financial aid office whether the repairs could count and what documents they'd need.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 3, Ch. 2: Cost of Attendance (Budget)

question: Can you guarantee I won't owe anything if I withdraw from all my classes now?
answer: I can't guarantee that, because the outcome depends on your aid, how far into the term you are, and your school's refund policy. The federal R2T4 calculation decides how much aid you earned based on the share of the term you completed, and your school's own policy decides what you still owe for tuition and other charges. Ask your financial aid office to run an estimate and the bursar to explain the refund policy before you withdraw.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 5, Ch. 1: General Requirements for Withdrawals and the Return of Title IV Funds
